items.text: give credit where credit is due
items.form: give credit where credit is due
items.meaning: Acknowledge someone's achievement or contribution, especially if it might otherwise be overlooked.
items.example: I have to give credit where credit is due; your presentation really turned the project around.
items.plain: Your presentation really turned the project around, and I want to acknowledge that.
items.note: Used to ensure someone gets recognition. Often said by a manager or colleague.

items.meaning: To do more than what is expected or required.
items.example: Sarah really went above and beyond on this report, adding extra research that wasn't requested.
items.plain: Sarah did more than expected on this report, adding extra research.
items.note: A common way to praise exceptional effort. Positive and appreciative.

items.meaning: Express sincere gratitude for someone's effort or contribution.
items.example: I really appreciate your quick turnaround on those edits; it helped us meet the deadline.
items.plain: Thank you for editing those so quickly; it helped us meet the deadline.
items.note: A very common and polite way to express thanks for specific actions.

items.meaning: A task or piece of work that has been completed successfully and to a high standard.
items.example: I just wanted to say congratulations on a job well done with the new client proposal.
items.plain: Congratulations on successfully completing the new client proposal.
items.note: A standard, positive phrase for acknowledging good work. Can be formal or informal.

items.meaning: Encourage someone to continue performing at their current high standard.
items.example: Your analysis was excellent this quarter, so keep up the good work.
items.plain: Your analysis was excellent this quarter; continue doing well.
items.note: A common, encouraging phrase, often used by managers.

items.meaning: Performed better than what was anticipated or hoped for.
items.example: Your performance on the recent project truly exceeded expectations, especially under pressure.
items.plain: You performed better than expected on the recent project, especially under pressure.
items.note: A strong positive phrase, often used in formal reviews or significant praise.

items.meaning: Someone or something that is very valuable or useful.
items.example: Your problem-solving skills make you a real asset to the team, especially during challenging times.
items.plain: Your problem-solving skills are very valuable to the team during challenging times.
items.note: A strong compliment, highlighting someone's value to a group or organization.

items.meaning: To highlight or draw attention to something, often positive.
items.example: I want to shine a light on Mark's innovative approach to the budget, which saved us money.
items.plain: I want to highlight Mark's innovative approach to the budget, which saved us money.
items.note: Used to bring attention to a specific positive contribution.

items.meaning: Acknowledge that someone has made a valid, insightful, or useful observation.
items.example: That's a great point about the timeline; I hadn't considered the external dependencies.
items.plain: You made a good observation about the timeline; I hadn't considered the external dependencies.
items.note: A common, positive way to acknowledge someone's contribution in a discussion.

items.meaning: Express admiration for someone's skill, effort, or achievement.
items.example: I'm impressed by how quickly you adapted to the new software, despite the steep learning curve.
items.plain: I admire how quickly you adapted to the new software, despite it being difficult to learn.
items.note: A direct and sincere way to give praise.

items.meaning: Introduce a piece of advice or an alternative idea in a polite way.
items.example: I have a suggestion regarding the report's structure that might make it clearer for readers.
items.plain: I want to suggest something about the report's structure to make it clearer.
items.note: A polite and common way to offer advice without sounding demanding.

items.meaning: Used to ensure understanding or to clarify a point, often before giving feedback.
items.example: Just to be clear, I think the content is strong, but the formatting needs some adjustments.
items.plain: I want to make sure you understand: the content is strong, but the formatting needs adjustments.
items.note: Used to preface a clarification or to ensure no misunderstanding.

items.meaning: Introduce a single, specific worry or issue you have.
items.example: My only concern is that the proposed solution might not be scalable for future growth.
items.plain: I am only worried that the proposed solution might not be scalable for future growth.
items.note: A polite way to express a reservation, often implying other aspects are fine.

items.meaning: Suggest an action or approach in a gentle, non-directive way.
items.example: It might be helpful to include more data points to support your conclusions in the next draft.
items.plain: Including more data points to support your conclusions in the next draft could be useful.
items.note: A very soft and indirect way to give advice or suggest an improvement.

items.meaning: Express uncertainty or introduce a gentle critique or question.
items.example: I'm not sure if the current approach fully addresses the client's core needs.
items.plain: I question whether the current approach fully addresses the client's core needs.
items.note: A polite way to express doubt or suggest a potential problem.

items.meaning: Introduce your personal opinion or viewpoint, acknowledging it might differ from others.
items.example: From my perspective, the presentation could benefit from a stronger opening statement.
items.plain: In my opinion, the presentation could benefit from a stronger opening statement.
items.note: Used to soften feedback by framing it as a personal view, not an absolute truth.

items.meaning: Introduce a frank or direct statement, often one that might be slightly critical.
items.example: To be honest, I think we need to reconsider the entire strategy for this quarter.
items.plain: Frankly, I think we need to reconsider the entire strategy for this quarter.
items.note: Can soften or strengthen a statement. Use carefully, as it can imply previous dishonesty.

items.meaning: Introduce a topic for discussion, often a concern or a point that needs attention.
items.example: I'd like to raise a point about the budget allocation for the upcoming marketing campaign.
items.plain: I want to discuss the budget allocation for the upcoming marketing campaign.
items.note: A polite and professional way to introduce a topic, often a concern.

items.meaning: Areas where something could be made better or more effective.
items.example: While the initial draft was good, there's still room for improvement in the data visualization.
items.plain: While the initial draft was good, the data visualization could still be better.
items.note: A common, polite, and indirect way to suggest that something is not perfect.

items.meaning: To fail to meet an expectation or standard.
items.example: Unfortunately, the final report fell short of the quality we usually expect from this team.
items.plain: Unfortunately, the final report was not as good as the quality we usually expect.
items.note: A polite but clear way to indicate something didn't meet standards.

items.meaning: Introduce a contrasting point or an alternative perspective.
items.example: The design is innovative; on the other hand, it might be too complex for our target audience.
items.plain: The design is innovative, but it might be too complex for our target audience.
items.note: Used to balance positive feedback with constructive criticism.

items.meaning: A polite but firm way to introduce a disagreement or criticism.
items.example: With all due respect, I think your analysis overlooks some key market trends.
items.plain: I respectfully disagree; I think your analysis overlooks some key market trends.
items.note: A formal phrase, often used when disagreeing with someone in authority. Can sound a bit confrontational.

items.meaning: Express a mild worry or reservation about something.
items.example: I'm a bit concerned about the tight deadline for this project, given our current workload.
items.plain: I'm slightly worried about the tight deadline for this project, given our current workload.
items.note: A common and polite way to express a reservation without being overly negative.

items.meaning: Introduce a personal observation or opinion, often a gentle suggestion or critique.
items.example: It seems to me that the new process adds an unnecessary step, slowing things down.
items.plain: I think the new process adds an unnecessary step, slowing things down.
items.note: A polite and indirect way to offer an opinion or observation.

items.meaning: Offer advice or a recommendation in a polite and indirect manner.
items.example: I would suggest that we revisit the budget figures before presenting them to the board.
items.plain: I recommend that we revisit the budget figures before presenting them to the board.
items.note: A polite and professional way to give advice.

items.meaning: To draw attention to a specific fact or detail.
items.example: I wanted to point out that the data in section three seems inconsistent with the appendix.
items.plain: I wanted to mention that the data in section three seems inconsistent with the appendix.
items.note: Used to highlight a specific detail, often a problem or discrepancy.

items.meaning: Remember or consider a particular fact or circumstance.
items.example: When giving feedback, bear in mind that everyone responds differently to criticism.
items.plain: When giving feedback, remember that everyone responds differently to criticism.
items.note: Used to remind someone of an important consideration.

items.meaning: For use or consideration at a later time, often when giving advice.
items.example: For future reference, it's better to confirm meeting times with all attendees beforehand.
items.plain: In the future, it's better to confirm meeting times with all attendees beforehand.
items.note: Used to give advice that applies to similar situations in the future.

items.meaning: Express a degree of doubt or uncertainty, often preceding a gentle critique.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure this solution aligns with our long-term strategic goals.
items.plain: I doubt this solution fully aligns with our long-term strategic goals.
items.note: A polite and indirect way to express a reservation or disagreement.

items.meaning: Suggest that something is a good idea to consider or try.
items.example: It might be worth exploring alternative software options before making a final decision.
items.plain: We should consider exploring alternative software options before making a final decision.
items.note: A gentle way to suggest an action or idea.

items.meaning: Introduce a suggestion, advice, or help in a polite manner.
items.example: I'd like to offer some thoughts on how we could streamline the onboarding process.
items.plain: I want to share some thoughts on how we could streamline the onboarding process.
items.note: A polite and professional way to give advice or suggestions.

items.meaning: A small additional amount or degree, often used to soften a suggestion for improvement.
items.example: The report needs a bit more detail in the executive summary to be truly effective.
items.plain: The report needs more detail in the executive summary to be truly effective.
items.note: Used to soften a request for improvement, making it sound less demanding.

items.meaning: Indicates that something is not perfect and has potential for betterment.
items.example: The communication between departments could be improved to avoid future misunderstandings.
items.plain: The communication between departments needs to get better to avoid future misunderstandings.
items.note: A common and polite way to suggest an area for development.

items.meaning: Offer a strong suggestion or piece of advice.
items.example: I'd recommend that you review the client's previous feedback before finalizing the design.
items.plain: I advise you to review the client's previous feedback before finalizing the design.
items.note: A professional way to give advice, slightly stronger than "I would suggest".

items.meaning: To consider particular facts, circumstances, or opinions when making a decision.
items.example: We need to take into account the team's workload before assigning any new tasks.
items.plain: We need to consider the team's workload before assigning any new tasks.
items.note: A common phrase for emphasizing the need to consider all relevant factors.

items.meaning: Introduce a question or a gentle suggestion in a tentative way.
items.example: I'm wondering if we should consider a different approach to reach a wider audience.
items.plain: Should we consider a different approach to reach a wider audience?
items.note: A polite and indirect way to ask a question or make a suggestion.

items.meaning: Introduce an important piece of information or a relevant fact.
items.example: It's worth noting that the project timeline has shifted, impacting our delivery date.
items.plain: We should note that the project timeline has shifted, impacting our delivery date.
items.note: Used to highlight an important detail, often when giving an update or context.

items.meaning: Introduce the purpose of your communication, often to give feedback or make a point.
items.example: I just wanted to mention that the report contains a few minor typos.
items.plain: I wanted to mention that the report contains a few minor typos.
items.note: A common, informal way to introduce a point, often a gentle one.

items.meaning: Introduce a personal viewpoint or judgment.
items.example: In my opinion, the new marketing campaign needs a stronger call to action.
items.plain: I think the new marketing campaign needs a stronger call to action.
items.note: A standard way to express a personal view. Can be softened with "humble" or "honest".

items.meaning: Introduce a suggestion or recommendation for a course of action.
items.example: I think we should schedule a follow-up meeting to discuss these points further.
items.plain: We should schedule a follow-up meeting to discuss these points further.
items.note: A direct but collaborative way to suggest an action.

items.meaning: Acknowledge and thank someone for their comments or critique.
items.example: I appreciate your feedback on the presentation; I'll definitely consider your points.
items.plain: Thank you for your comments on the presentation; I'll definitely consider your points.
items.note: A polite and professional way to acknowledge feedback, even if you don't fully agree.

items.meaning: To understand and accept an idea or suggestion, often for future action.
items.example: That's a valid point about the timeline; I'll take that on board for the next project.
items.plain: That's a valid point about the timeline; I'll consider it for the next project.
items.note: A common British English phrase for accepting advice or criticism.

items.meaning: Acknowledge and understand someone's point, even if you don't fully agree.
items.example: I hear what you're saying about the budget constraints, but we need to invest in quality.
items.plain: I understand your point about the budget constraints, but we need to invest in quality.
items.note: Used to show you've listened, often before presenting a counter-argument.

items.meaning: Acknowledge that someone's observation or criticism is reasonable and valid.
items.example: That's a fair point about the lack of communication; we definitely need to improve there.
items.plain: You're right about the lack of communication; we definitely need to improve there.
items.note: A common way to acknowledge valid criticism without necessarily agreeing to change.

items.meaning: Promise to investigate or examine a matter further.
items.example: You mentioned a discrepancy in the figures; I'll look into that right away.
items.plain: You mentioned a discrepancy in the figures; I will investigate it right away.
items.note: A common, reassuring response when someone raises a problem.

items.meaning: Acknowledge someone's worry or issue, showing empathy.
items.example: I understand your concern about the project's scope, and we're actively managing it.
items.plain: I recognize your worry about the project's scope, and we're actively managing it.
items.note: A polite and empathetic way to respond to someone's worry.

items.meaning: Express gratitude for someone raising an issue or topic.
items.example: Thanks for bringing that up; it's an important point we need to address in the meeting.
items.plain: I appreciate you mentioning that; it's an important point we need to address.
items.note: A polite and common way to acknowledge someone for raising a topic.

items.meaning: Promise to remember a piece of information or advice for future consideration.
items.example: Your suggestion about the new software is helpful; I'll keep that in mind for our next review.
items.plain: Your suggestion about the new software is helpful; I'll remember it for our next review.
items.note: A common, polite way to acknowledge advice without committing to immediate action.

items.meaning: Acknowledge that someone has made a valid or reasonable argument.
items.example: You've got a point about the tight deadline; we might need to re-prioritize some tasks.
items.plain: You're right about the tight deadline; we might need to re-prioritize some tasks.
items.note: An informal but common way to concede a point in a discussion.

items.meaning: Indicate that you understand someone's perspective or explanation.
items.example: I see what you mean about the client's expectations; they are quite high for this project.
items.plain: I understand your point about the client's expectations; they are quite high.
items.note: A common, neutral phrase to show understanding.

items.meaning: Introduce an explanation to make something clearer or correct a misunderstanding.
items.example: Let me clarify my previous statement; I meant the *initial* proposal, not the final one.
items.plain: I want to make my previous statement clearer; I meant the *initial* proposal.
items.note: Used when you need to explain something further or correct a misinterpretation.

items.meaning: Accept complete blame or accountability for a mistake or outcome.
items.example: I take full responsibility for the oversight in the budget calculations; it won't happen again.
items.plain: I am completely responsible for the oversight in the budget calculations; it won't happen again.
items.note: A strong and direct way to admit fault.

items.meaning: Indicate willingness to hear and consider new ideas or advice.
items.example: I'm open to suggestions on how we can improve our team's communication flow.
items.plain: I am willing to hear new ideas on how we can improve our team's communication flow.
items.note: A positive and collaborative phrase, inviting input from others.

items.meaning: Promise to take a specific action or ensure something happens.
items.example: I'll make sure to double-check all the figures before submitting the final report.
items.plain: I will double-check all the figures before submitting the final report.
items.note: A common way to reassure someone that you will address their point.

items.text: I'm glad you brought that up
items.form: I'm glad you brought that up
items.meaning: Express appreciation that someone raised a particular topic or issue.
items.example: I'm glad you brought that up; it's an important point we need to discuss as a team.
items.plain: I'm happy you mentioned that; it's an important point we need to discuss as a team.
items.note: A positive way to acknowledge someone for raising a relevant issue.

items.meaning: Promise to try as hard as possible to achieve something.
items.example: I'll do my best to incorporate your feedback into the next iteration of the design.
items.plain: I will try my hardest to incorporate your feedback into the next iteration of the design.
items.note: A common, reassuring phrase when committing to an effort.

items.meaning: Acknowledge that you understand and accept a criticism or suggestion.
items.example: Point taken; I should have communicated the changes more clearly to the whole team.
items.plain: I understand your criticism; I should have communicated the changes more clearly.
items.note: A concise and direct way to acknowledge and accept a valid point.

items.meaning: Promise to monitor or pay attention to a situation or issue.
items.example: I'll keep an eye on the project's progress to ensure we stay within budget.
items.plain: I will monitor the project's progress to ensure we stay within budget.
items.note: A common way to reassure someone that you will be vigilant about something.

items.meaning: Indicate that you are currently addressing or trying to resolve an issue.
items.example: You mentioned the report's formatting issues; I'm working on it and expect to finish soon.
items.plain: You mentioned the report's formatting issues; I am currently fixing them.
items.note: A common, informal response to indicate progress on a task or issue.

items.meaning: Promise to respond or provide more information at a later time.
items.example: That's a complex question about the new policy; I'll get back to you with a detailed answer.
items.plain: That's a complex question about the new policy; I will give you a detailed answer later.
items.note: A common, polite way to defer an answer when you need more time or information.

items.meaning: Introduce a topic for discussion in a direct and collaborative way.
items.example: Let's talk about the recent project's outcomes and what we can learn from them.
items.plain: We should discuss the recent project's outcomes and what we can learn from them.
items.note: A common, direct, and inclusive way to start a discussion.

items.meaning: Introduce a topic briefly or mention it as part of a broader discussion.
items.example: I wanted to touch on your performance this quarter, specifically your excellent client communication.
items.plain: I wanted to briefly mention your performance this quarter, specifically your excellent client communication.
items.note: A polite way to introduce a topic, often implying it's one of several points.

items.meaning: Introduce a summary of the main points that have been discussed.
items.example: To sum up, the project was successful, but we need to improve our internal communication.
items.plain: In summary, the project was successful, but we need to improve our internal communication.
items.note: A common phrase for concluding a discussion or presentation.

items.meaning: Considering most aspects of a situation; generally.
items.example: On the whole, the team's performance this year has been outstanding, with only minor issues.
items.plain: Generally, the team's performance this year has been outstanding, with only minor issues.
items.note: Used to give a general assessment, often before mentioning specific details.

items.meaning: Taking all factors and circumstances into account.
items.example: All things considered, the launch went smoothly, despite the initial technical glitches.
items.plain: Considering all factors, the launch went smoothly, despite the initial technical glitches.
items.note: Used to introduce a balanced conclusion after weighing various factors.

items.meaning: Usually; mostly; considering the overall situation rather than specific details.
items.example: In general, your work is excellent, but this particular report needs more attention to detail.
items.plain: Usually, your work is excellent, but this particular report needs more attention to detail.
items.note: Used to give a broad overview before diving into specifics.

items.meaning: Explain the main point or intention behind what you are saying.
items.example: What I'm getting at is that we need a clearer strategy for client retention next quarter.
items.plain: My main point is that we need a clearer strategy for client retention next quarter.
items.note: Used to clarify your main message, especially if you've been indirect.

items.meaning: State the most important fact or the essential truth of a situation.
items.example: The bottom line is, we need to improve our efficiency to meet these new targets.
items.plain: The most important thing is that we need to improve our efficiency to meet these new targets.
items.note: Used to emphasize the crucial point or outcome. Can be quite direct.

items.meaning: Introduce a mitigating factor or a balanced perspective, often to defend someone or something.
items.example: To be fair, the team was under immense pressure, which explains some of the delays.
items.plain: We should acknowledge that the team was under immense pressure, which explains some delays.
items.note: Used to introduce a point that balances a previous criticism or negative statement.

items.meaning: Introduce a piece of advice or an opinion that you think might be helpful, but might not be.
items.example: For what it's worth, I think a different color scheme would make the slides more engaging.
items.plain: I think a different color scheme would make the slides more engaging, but it's just my opinion.
items.note: Used to offer a suggestion or opinion humbly, acknowledging it might not be highly valued.

items.meaning: State your intention to speak concisely or to summarize quickly.
items.example: I'll keep it brief, but I wanted to highlight a few key successes from this quarter.
items.plain: I will speak briefly, but I wanted to highlight a few key successes from this quarter.
items.note: Used to signal that you won't take up much time, often at the start of a short speech.

items.meaning: Suggest transitioning to the next topic or agenda item.
items.example: Now that we've discussed the budget, let's move on to the marketing strategy.
items.plain: Now that we've discussed the budget, let's proceed to the marketing strategy.
items.note: A common phrase for guiding a discussion or meeting.

items.meaning: Introduce an additional point or piece of information to a discussion.
items.example: I'd like to add that the team's collaboration on this project was exceptional.
items.plain: I want to also say that the team's collaboration on this project was exceptional.
items.note: A polite way to contribute an extra point to a conversation.

items.meaning: Emphasize that you are about to state your true and frank opinion.
items.example: To be perfectly honest, I don't think the current timeline is realistic for this complex task.
items.plain: Frankly, I don't think the current timeline is realistic for this complex task.
items.note: A stronger version of "to be honest," indicating a very direct or potentially difficult truth.

items.meaning: Introduce your personal interpretation or understanding of a situation.
items.example: The way I see it, we have two main options for resolving this client issue.
items.plain: In my opinion, we have two main options for resolving this client issue.
items.note: A common way to present your perspective, often before offering a solution.

items.meaning: Emphasize the significance or necessity of a particular action or consideration.
items.example: It's important to acknowledge the hard work everyone put into this successful launch.
items.plain: We must acknowledge the hard work everyone put into this successful launch.
items.note: Used to highlight the significance of something, often when giving praise or advice.

items.text: I just wanted to check in
items.form: I just wanted to check in
items.meaning: Initiate a conversation to see how someone is doing or to get an update.
items.example: I just wanted to check in on your progress with the new software implementation.
items.plain: I wanted to ask about your progress with the new software implementation.
items.note: A common, informal way to start a conversation, often for a quick update or to offer support.

items.meaning: Offer assistance or support willingly.
items.example: If you need any guidance on the new project, I'm happy to help.
items.plain: If you need any guidance on the new project, I will gladly assist you.
items.note: A common and polite way to offer support.

items.meaning: Express strong belief or assurance about a future outcome or fact.
items.example: I'm confident that with a few adjustments, this proposal will be very strong.
items.plain: I strongly believe that with a few adjustments, this proposal will be very strong.
items.note: Used to express certainty or positive expectation, often when giving encouraging feedback.

items.meaning: Suggest directing attention and effort towards a specific area or task.
items.example: For the next quarter, let's focus on improving our customer satisfaction scores.
items.plain: For the next quarter, we should concentrate on improving our customer satisfaction scores.
items.note: A common way to guide a team or individual towards a specific goal.

items.meaning: Express satisfaction or happiness about something.
items.example: I'm pleased with the progress you've made on the project this week.
items.plain: I'm happy about the progress you've made on the project this week.
items.note: A common and positive way to give feedback, often from a manager.

items.meaning: Praise someone for performing a task very well.
items.example: You did a great job handling that difficult client situation yesterday.
items.plain: You handled that difficult client situation very well yesterday.
items.note: A common, direct, and enthusiastic way to give praise.

items.meaning: Express admiration for someone's qualities or achievements.
items.example: I'm impressed with your ability to manage multiple tasks effectively.
items.plain: I admire your ability to manage multiple tasks effectively.
items.note: A sincere way to give praise, focusing on a skill or quality.

items.meaning: Congratulate someone on a specific achievement or successful action.
items.example: Well done on securing that new contract; it's a significant win for the team.
items.plain: Congratulations on securing that new contract; it's a significant win.
items.note: A common and direct way to praise a specific accomplishment.

items.meaning: Praise someone for performing exceptionally well in a particular area.
items.example: You've really excelled at client presentations this quarter, showing great confidence.
items.plain: You've performed exceptionally well at client presentations this quarter.
items.note: A strong compliment, highlighting outstanding performance in a specific skill.

items.meaning: Express pleasure or satisfaction about an observation or development.
items.example: I'm happy to see your proactive approach to problem-solving on this project.
items.plain: I'm pleased by your proactive approach to problem-solving on this project.
items.note: A positive and encouraging way to give feedback, often from a manager.

items.meaning: Acknowledge that an idea is good, well-thought-out, and practical.
items.example: That's a solid idea for improving our workflow; let's explore it further.
items.plain: That's a good idea for improving our workflow; let's explore it further.
items.note: A common, positive way to affirm a good suggestion.

items.meaning: Express strong admiration for someone's qualities or actions.
items.example: I'm really impressed by your resilience in handling the unexpected challenges.
items.plain: I truly admire your resilience in handling the unexpected challenges.
items.note: A stronger version of "I'm impressed by," conveying deeper admiration.

items.meaning: Introduce a polite suggestion for an improvement or desired outcome.
items.example: It would be great if you could provide more regular updates on your progress.
items.plain: Please provide more regular updates on your progress; that would be helpful.
items.note: A polite and indirect way to make a request or suggest an improvement.

items.meaning: Express a desire for a particular action or outcome, often as a suggestion.
items.example: I'd like to see more proactive communication from the team on potential roadblocks.
items.plain: I want to see more proactive communication from the team on potential roadblocks.
items.note: A common way for a manager to express expectations or desired changes.

items.meaning: Suggest an alternative approach or action that could be more effective.
items.example: It might be better to schedule a separate meeting for brainstorming new ideas.
items.plain: Scheduling a separate meeting for brainstorming new ideas could be better.
items.note: A gentle and indirect way to suggest an alternative or improvement.

items.meaning: Express a slight concern or apprehension about something.
items.example: I'm a little worried about the potential impact of these changes on team morale.
items.plain: I'm slightly concerned about the potential impact of these changes on team morale.
items.note: A common and polite way to express a mild reservation.

items.meaning: Indicate that a particular issue or problem requires attention and action.
items.example: We need to address the inconsistencies in the data before the final presentation.
items.plain: We must deal with the inconsistencies in the data before the final presentation.
items.note: A direct and clear way to highlight a problem that requires resolution.

items.meaning: Express a degree of doubt or disagreement with an idea or statement.
items.example: I'm not entirely convinced that this strategy will yield the desired results.
items.plain: I doubt this strategy will fully achieve the desired results.
items.note: A polite and indirect way to express skepticism or disagreement.

items.meaning: Highlight a chance for improvement or development.
items.example: There's an opportunity to streamline this process and save significant time.
items.plain: We have a chance to streamline this process and save significant time.
items.note: A positive way to frame a suggestion for improvement, focusing on potential gains.

items.meaning: Suggest or advise someone to take a particular action.
items.example: I'd encourage you to seek out more training opportunities in project management.
items.plain: I advise you to seek out more training opportunities in project management.
items.note: A polite and supportive way to give advice or suggest development.

items.meaning: Express uncertainty or reservation regarding a specific aspect.
items.example: I'm not sure about the feasibility of implementing this new system by next month.
items.plain: I'm uncertain about whether we can implement this new system by next month.
items.note: A common and polite way to express doubt or a potential problem.

items.meaning: Promise to think about a suggestion or piece of feedback.
items.example: Your point about the budget is noted; I'll take that into consideration for the next phase.
items.plain: Your point about the budget is noted; I will think about it for the next phase.
items.note: A polite way to acknowledge feedback without committing to immediate action.

items.text: I appreciate you pointing that out
items.form: I appreciate you pointing that out
items.meaning: Thank someone for drawing attention to a specific detail or issue.
items.example: I appreciate you pointing that out; I hadn't noticed the error in the calculations.
items.plain: Thank you for mentioning that; I hadn't noticed the error in the calculations.
items.note: A polite and common way to thank someone for highlighting a detail, often a mistake.

items.meaning: Express complete agreement with someone's statement or observation.
items.example: You're absolutely right; we should have involved the legal team earlier in the process.
items.plain: You are completely correct; we should have involved the legal team earlier.
items.note: A strong and direct way to agree with someone, often acknowledging a mistake.

items.text: I'll make a note of that
items.form: I'll make a note of that
items.meaning: Promise to record a piece of information or a suggestion.
items.example: That's a good idea for the next meeting agenda; I'll make a note of that.
items.plain: That's a good idea for the next meeting agenda; I will write it down.
items.note: A common, reassuring phrase indicating that a point has been heard and will be remembered.

items.meaning: Promise to take further action or investigate a matter.
items.example: You raised a question about the client's budget; I'll follow up on that and get back to you.
items.plain: You raised a question about the client's budget; I will investigate it and respond.
items.note: A common, professional way to commit to taking action on an issue.

items.meaning: Promise to definitely take a specific action.
items.example: I'll be sure to include your feedback in the revised project proposal.
items.plain: I will definitely include your feedback in the revised project proposal.
items.note: A strong commitment to perform an action.

items.meaning: Express strong dedication or promise to a particular goal or action.
items.example: I'm committed to improving my time management skills after this feedback session.
items.plain: I promise to improve my time management skills after this feedback session.
items.note: A strong statement of dedication, often used when accepting criticism.

items.meaning: Promise to make an effort to improve a specific behavior or quality.
items.example: I'll try to be more proactive in communicating updates to the team moving forward.
items.plain: I will make an effort to communicate updates to the team more proactively.
items.note: A common way to respond to constructive criticism by committing to change.

items.meaning: Promise to address or improve a specific area or task.
items.example: You mentioned my presentation style; I'll work on that to make it more engaging.
items.plain: You mentioned my presentation style; I will try to improve it.
items.note: A common, concise way to accept criticism and commit to improvement.

items.meaning: Promise to provide regular information about progress or developments.
items.example: Regarding the software bug, I'll keep you updated on our progress in resolving it.
items.plain: Regarding the software bug, I will regularly inform you about our progress.
items.note: A common, reassuring phrase used to manage expectations and maintain communication.

items.meaning: Express deep appreciation or thankfulness for something.
items.example: I'm grateful for your honest feedback; it helps me grow professionally.
items.plain: I appreciate your honest feedback; it helps me grow professionally.
items.note: A sincere way to express thanks, especially for valuable input.

items.meaning: Indicate that you are actively implementing measures to achieve a goal or address an issue.
items.example: I'm taking steps to improve my project planning after reviewing your comments.
items.plain: I am actively working to improve my project planning after reviewing your comments.
items.note: Used to show proactive engagement in addressing feedback or making improvements.

items.meaning: Express strong belief in the ability of a group to achieve something.
items.example: I'm confident we can overcome these challenges with a collaborative approach.
items.plain: I strongly believe we can overcome these challenges with a collaborative approach.
items.note: Used to express optimism and encourage teamwork, often after discussing issues.

items.meaning: Express anticipation or eagerness for a future event or outcome.
items.example: I'm looking forward to seeing the improvements in the next version of the report.
items.plain: I'm excited to see the improvements in the next version of the report.
items.note: A positive way to express expectation, often after giving constructive feedback.

items.meaning: Offer to talk further about a topic or issue.
items.example: If you have more questions about the new policy, I'm happy to discuss them.
items.plain: If you have more questions about the new policy, I will gladly discuss them.
items.note: A polite and open offer to continue a conversation or provide more information.

items.meaning: Offer help and encouragement to someone.
items.example: As you implement these changes, remember I'm here to support you every step of the way.
items.plain: As you implement these changes, remember I will help you every step of the way.
items.note: A common, reassuring phrase from a manager or mentor offering assistance.

items.meaning: Express certainty or strong belief about a fact or outcome.
items.example: I'm sure that with a bit more practice, you'll master the new software.
items.plain: I believe that with a bit more practice, you'll master the new software.
items.note: Used to express confidence, often when giving encouraging feedback.

items.meaning: Introduce positive news or a positive development.
items.example: I'm pleased to announce that the team successfully met all project milestones.
items.plain: I'm happy to share that the team successfully met all project milestones.
items.note: A formal and positive way to deliver good news, often in a team setting.

items.meaning: Express happiness or relief about information received.
items.example: I'm glad to hear that you've already started implementing the feedback.
items.plain: I'm happy to know that you've already started implementing the feedback.
items.note: A common, positive response to good news or progress.

items.meaning: Express satisfaction or contentment with something.
items.example: I'm happy with the overall quality of the final report, despite minor issues.
items.plain: I'm satisfied with the overall quality of the final report, despite minor issues.
items.note: A common and direct way to express positive feedback.
